name: Poverty Point
writeup: Between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, hunter-fisher-gatherers built six curved earthen ridges and several mounds here around a broad, flat plaza. Excavation and remote sensing show that rings of very large wooden posts once stood in that plaza. No musical instruments have been reported from the site, and nobody knows what was sung or danced here. UNESCO describes the earthworks as made and used for residential and ceremonial purposes, so archaeologists infer that people gathered in the plaza for shared events. That inference, not any surviving sound, is why the map's story of Louisiana gatherings begins at Poverty Point.
sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point <https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1435/> | 64 Parishes, Poverty Point <https://64parishes.org/entry/poverty-point> | Louisiana Office of Tourism, History and Artifacts of Poverty Point <https://www.povertypoint.us/history-artifacts-poverty-point>

name: Marksville Prehistoric Indian Site
writeup: About 2,000 years ago people raised six mounds and a long semicircular earthen embankment here, a ceremonial center that gives the Marksville culture (about 1 to 400 CE) its name. The one burial mound held thirty-six people. At the related Crooks site, archaeologists found clusters of pebbles in graves that they interpret as the surviving contents of rattles whose casings rotted away, a rare physical hint of sound-making in ancient Louisiana. No such rattles are reported from Marksville itself, and the ceremonies held inside the embankment are inferred from the earthworks and burials. The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe now manages the site.
sources: 64 Parishes, Marksville Culture by Rebecca Saunders <https://64parishes.org/entry/marksville-culture> | Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, article on the Marksville site reposted from NOLA.com <https://www.tunicabiloxi.org/this-archaeological-site-drew-pilgrims-2000-years-ago-now-there-are-big-plans-for-its-future/>

name: Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana
writeup: The Chitimacha say they have always been here, and the tribe still lives on part of its homeland along Bayou Teche; the 1500 date only marks the edge of the written record. When Frances Densmore visited in January 1933, Chief Benjamin Paul, Christine Paul and Delphine Decloux described a cane flute with four holes on top and one beneath, a drum of deerskin stretched over a clay pot, an alligator-skin rattle, and a dance held when the chief blessed the seed corn. Densmore could record no old songs and wrote that they had been lost. The tribe carries its culture forward today through oral tradition, language work and its museum.
sources: Frances Densmore, A Search for Songs among the Chitimacha Indians in Louisiana, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 133 (1943), full text <https://archive.org/stream/bulletin1331943smit/bulletin1331943smit_djvu.txt> | Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana, Tribal History <https://chitimacha.gov/history-culture/tribal-history> | Louisiana Office of Tourism, Chitimacha Museum <https://www.explorelouisiana.com/museums/chitimacha-museum>

name: Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana
writeup: The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe is the successor to the Tunica, Biloxi, Ofo and Avoyel peoples, whose songs are far older than any written account; 1500 is a placeholder for that deeper past. The Tunica moved down the Mississippi in 1706 and have made Marksville their main settlement since the 1780s. Today the tribe's Language and Culture Revitalization Program, based at the Cultural and Educational Resources Center, teaches the Tunica language through traditional songs and stories, and children learn traditional and powwow songs and dances. Each spring the tribe hosts a powwow on the reservation with intertribal dance competitions. Songs and stories passed down by community elders remain the core of this work.
sources: 64 Parishes, Tunica-Biloxi Tribe <https://64parishes.org/entry/tunica-biloxi-tribe> | Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, Language and Culture Revitalization Program <https://tunicabiloxi.org/tribal-info/departments/language-culture-revitalization-program> | Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, 26th Annual Pow Wow <https://www.tunicabiloxi.org/tunica-biloxi-tribe-of-louisiana-celebrates-the-success-of-26th-annual-pow-wow-2/>

name: Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana
writeup: The Koasati, or Coushatta, had migrated into Louisiana by 1795 and acquired their present lands near Elton in 1884; their song and dance traditions are much older than that move. The tribe describes the Stomp Dance as danced counter-clockwise around a fire at night, with men calling the songs and setting the pace and women keeping rhythm with turtle shakers, the smoke carrying prayers upward. The tribe notes that few members now know the original dances and songs, and it is working to pass them on. Dances such as the Round Dance and the Swan Dance are performed today, and the tribe hosts a large annual powwow.
listen_1_label: Coushatta Round Dance and Swan Dance videos (National Park Service, Jean Lafitte NHP)
sources: Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, Coushatta Powwow <https://coushattapowwow.com/> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Keeping It Alive: Koasati Crafts and Storytelling <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Virtual_Books/Keeping_It/creole_book_keep_koas.html> | National Park Service, Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana <https://www.nps.gov/jela/learn/coushatta-tribe-of-louisiana.htm>

name: United Houma Nation
writeup: La Salle recorded a Houma village in 1682, and the Houma later moved south into the bayou country of Terrebonne and Lafourche, where most citizens live now. Their music is older than those records; 1500 simply marks the approach of the written record. Tribal leaders describe songs about the land, the water and past leaders, many of them prayer songs, sung in English, Choctaw and French and handed down by elders. Singers use hand drums and large hide drums, and a tribal administrator recalls that the Houma were traditionally stomp dancers with distinct ceremonial music. The nation gathers for an annual powwow. The point marks the tribal office in Houma.
sources: Garde Voir Ci (Nicholls State University), The Musical Backdrop <https://gardevoirci.nicholls.edu/2021/music/> | Garde Voir Ci (Nicholls State University), The Houma People <https://gardevoirci.nicholls.edu/2021/the-houma-people/> | United Houma Nation, About <https://unitedhoumanation.org/about/>

name: Adai Caddo Indian Nation Cultural Center
writeup: Northwest Louisiana is Caddo homeland, and Caddo music long predates the written record; 1500 is only a marker for that. Most Caddo people left Louisiana after 1835 and the Caddo Nation is now in Oklahoma, where the Drum Dance and Turkey Dance songs still recount tribal history, naming places such as Caddo Lake and the Ouachita River. Near Robeline, the Adai Caddo community keeps a cultural center and holds an annual powwow where members and visiting tribes from Texas and Oklahoma drum, sing and dance. Their chief describes the old dances as prayers, for rain or for the safe return of warriors.

name: St. Louis Cathedral (colonial parish church)
writeup: European art music took root in Louisiana through the military and the Catholic Church, and this site was its center. Pierre Fleurtel was musician and schoolmaster for the St. Louis parish in 1725, joined the next year by François Saucier; the first parish church here was completed in 1727. That building burned in 1788, and its replacement was dedicated as a cathedral in 1794. Vicente Llorca, who served as church musician until 1803, is the first composer known to have worked in Louisiana. Little colonial music survives on paper, so much of what was sung here is known only from records of the people who made it.
sources: 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana by Alfred E. Lemmon <https://64parishes.org/?p=691> | 64 Parishes, St. Louis Cathedral <https://64parishes.org/?p=37591>

name: Old Ursuline Convent
writeup: The Ursuline nuns reached New Orleans in 1727 and made music part of the schooling they gave girls. In 1754 a donor known only as Monsieur Nicollet sent them a bound manuscript, copied in 1736 by a scribe signing C. D., of 294 sacred songs that fit new devotional words to tunes by Lully, Couperin, Campra, Clérambault and others. It is the oldest known music manuscript in Louisiana and stayed with the Ursulines until The Historic New Orleans Collection acquired their archives in 1998. The convent on Chartres Street, finished in the early 1750s, is the building most closely tied to the book's arrival.
listen_1_label: Songs from the Ursuline manuscript performed by Le Concert Lorrain (The Historic New Orleans Collection)
sources: The Historic New Orleans Collection, Ursuline Music Manuscript <https://hnoc.org/research-collections/collection-highlights/ursuline-music-manuscript> | 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana by Alfred E. Lemmon <https://64parishes.org/?p=691> | Wikipedia, Old Ursuline Convent, New Orleans (building dates only) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Ursuline_Convent,_New_Orleans>

name: Théâtre St. Pierre (site)
writeup: New Orleans's first French-language theatre opened in October 1792, under Spanish rule, on St. Peter Street between Royal and Bourbon. On May 22, 1796 it staged André Grétry's Sylvain, the first opera known to have been performed in the city, which began an operatic tradition that New Orleans kept up almost without a break. The composer Joseph Arquier worked in the city from 1800 to 1803. The building is long gone and the point marks the block where it stood, not a surviving structure. Sources differ on the end: 64 Parishes says the theatre closed in 1803, while other accounts have it lingering until an 1810 auction.
sources: 64 Parishes, Opera and Ballet <https://64parishes.org/entry/opera-and-ballet> | 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana by Alfred E. Lemmon <https://64parishes.org/?p=691> | Wikipedia, Theatre de la Rue Saint Pierre (used for the 1810 date and block location) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_de_la_Rue_Saint_Pierre>

name: Congo Square
writeup: The 1724 Code Noir made Sunday a day without work for everyone in the colony, and enslaved Africans used it to gather, trade and make music in several places around the city. By the late 1740s this open ground behind the town was one of them, serving as a market and meeting place through the French and Spanish periods. An 1817 ordinance then confined such gatherings to this square, where hundreds danced the Bamboula, Calinda and Congo to gourd rattles and instruments modelled on African ones. The detailed eyewitness accounts date from after 1803; the colonial-era gatherings are documented more thinly. The start year is approximate.
sources: 64 Parishes, Congo Square <https://64parishes.org/entry/congo-square> | The Cultural Landscape Foundation, Congo Square <https://www.tclf.org/landscapes/congo-square> | New Orleans Historical, Congo Square: Mythology and Music <https://neworleanshistorical.org/items/show/745>

name: Los Isleños Museum Complex
writeup: Between 1778 and 1783 about 2,000 Canary Islanders came to Spanish Louisiana under Governor Bernardo de Gálvez. Of their four settlements, only the one in St. Bernard kept its Spanish identity, and later fishing villages such as Delacroix grew from it. The Isleños sang décimas, a Spanish form traceable to the fifteenth century, which here became sung stories about neighbours, scandals, tall tales and daily events. Irván Pérez, the best-known singer, received a National Heritage Fellowship in 1991 and died in 2008. The museum complex in St. Bernard interprets this heritage and hosts the annual Fiesta de los Isleños.
listen_1_label: La Décima de Wila, sung by Irván Pérez, 1988 (64 Parishes, Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities)
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, The Evolution of the Isleño Identity by Sara-Ann Harris <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/islenos.html> | Louisiana Office of Tourism, Los Isleños Museum <https://www.explorelouisiana.com/museums/los-islenos-museum> | 64 Parishes, La Décima de Wila (audio) <https://64parishes.org/entry-audio/la-decima-de-wila>

name: Acadian arrival at the Attakapas (Acadian Memorial)
writeup: In 1765, ten years after their deportation from Nova Scotia, Acadian exiles began reaching Louisiana, and 193 of them were sent to the Attakapas district, spreading out along the waterways around what became St. Martinville. No one wrote down what they sang that year. Folklorists do report that unaccompanied ballads were among the earliest music in French Louisiana, that Acadian families held on to theirs for generations, and that the fiddle was the first instrument in common use. From that stock of western French song, mixed over the following century with Native, African, Spanish and Anglo-American music, Cajun music grew. The Acadian Memorial stands beside Bayou Teche.
